claims.text: Formation of a protective Cr2O3, Al2O3, or SiO2 layer is crucial for high-temperature oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element alloys.
Cr, Al, and Si are protective-oxide-forming alloying elements.
Exposure to oxygen at high temperature causes formation of the proposed protective oxide layer.
The hypothesis is proposed for temperatures from 500 to 1000 °C.
The hypothesis is proposed for oxygen partial pressures from 0.1 to 1 atm.
A Cr2O3, Al2O3, or SiO2 layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Limiting oxygen diffusion through the protective layer reduces the alloy's oxidation rate.
The protective layer reduces formation of less-protective oxides.
Suppressing oxidation and less-protective oxides maintains overall alloy integrity.
Alloys forming the protective layer will have better oxidation resistance and a lower oxidation rate than the baseline.
Alloys forming the protective layer will undergo minimal degradation of strength and ductility.
Alloys lacking protective-oxide-forming elements or containing them at low concentration provide an appropriate baseline.
Pure metals are examples of materials without protective-oxide-forming elements.
The hypothesis may fail when protective-oxide-forming elements are present only at low concentrations.
The hypothesis may fail when another oxidation mechanism, such as volatile-oxide-induced breakaway oxidation, dominates.
The relationship among protective-layer formation, alloy composition, and microstructure is not fully understood.
Similar or better oxidation resistance in the baseline lacking protective-oxide-forming elements would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline treats pure metals as examples lacking protective-oxide-forming elements, while Cr, Al, and Si are themselves listed as protective-oxide-forming elements and can each be present as pure metals.
